Chapter 6: Expanding Beyond the Psalms—Praying Other Parts of Scripture
Once you feel at home praying through the Psalms, the next step is pretty exciting—why not explore the rest of the Bible as a source for your prayers? Sure, the Psalms are tailor-made for this, but every single book—whether it’s history, prophecy, wisdom, a gospel story, or a letter—has its own way of inviting us into a conversation with God.
The process is actually familiar: you read a passage slowly, pause when something catches your attention, and let that word or phrase spark a prayer. What changes is the variety—the tone, the style, and even the rhythm of what you’re reading. Maybe a moment from the Gospels fills you with gratitude for Jesus’ kindness. Or a parable nudges you to reflect on how you’re growing. And when you come across a command in one of the letters? That might inspire you to ask for help, or maybe even confess where you’re struggling.
Here are some practical ways to pray through different parts of Scripture:
Let’s start with narratives. These are the stories about real people—think Esther, Solomon, Abraham. As you read about their lives, imagine yourself in their shoes. Pray for the kind of courage Esther showed, the wisdom Solomon asked for, or the faith that carried Abraham forward. Their struggles and victories can become springboards for your own prayers.
Now, when you come across teachings and commands—those instructions that challenge us—take a moment to ask for strength to follow through. Or, if it’s tough, be honest with God about where you fall short. For instance, when you see “love your neighbor as yourself,” maybe you’ll pray for patience, or ask for a chance to forgive or serve someone in your life.
Next, there are promises and prophecies. When Scripture talks about God’s faithfulness or paints a picture of hope for the future, let that draw out gratitude or trust. Ask God to shape your hopes and expectations around His promises.
And what about those moments of lament or warning? When a passage expresses sorrow, or highlights injustice, bring your own griefs and concerns to God. Lift up those who are hurting, or ask for a heart that’s sensitive to the pain around you.
When you approach the Bible this way, it transforms from a static book into a living, breathing guide for prayer. You start to see connections and insights you might otherwise overlook, simply by responding honestly in prayer.
Take the story of the Good Samaritan, for example. Reading about that unexpected act of kindness might move you to pray for a neighbor who’s in need, or even ask for a heart that’s open to life’s little interruptions. Or maybe you come across a description of the early church’s generosity—and that sparks a prayer for more unity and compassion in your own community.
The key here? Stay open and responsive. Let the text shape the conversation. Not every verse will hit home, and that’s okay—just move on when something doesn’t resonate. Over time, you’ll find this practice adds new depth and variety to your prayers, as the full range of Scripture’s wisdom and beauty becomes a living part of your spiritual life.
